knowledgePoint.zh: 幻觉问题的技术解决方案与构建可信AI的路径
knowledgePoint.en: Technical approaches to the hallucination problem and building trustworthy AI

recallIntro.zh: 你想起那天罗素教授一进教室就把平板电脑递给了前排的一位同学，让他大声读屏幕上的一段文字。那段文字写得流畅、专业、充满细节——但每一个细节都是编造的。教授的表情很严肃：「这段话出自一个AI系统。它说的每一个字都错了，但你读的时候是不是觉得它挺可信的？」
recallIntro.en: You recall Prof. Russell handing his tablet to a student in the front row the moment he entered, asking them to read aloud a passage on the screen. The text was fluent, professional, full of detail — but every detail was fabricated. The professor's expression was grave: 「This passage was produced by an AI system. Every word is wrong, but didn't it sound credible as you were reading it?」

recallOutro.zh: 你合上笔记本，想起教授展示的那段编造的文字。你差一点就相信了，这才是最可怕的部分。一个不知道自己不知道什么的系统，配上一副无比自信的声音，构成了一种新型的欺骗。它甚至不是故意的。
recallOutro.en: You close your notebook, remembering that fabricated passage the professor showed. You almost believed it — and that's the most frightening part. A system that doesn't know what it doesn't know, paired with an utterly confident voice, is a new kind of deception — one that isn't even intentional.

text.zh: 罗素教授今天走进教室的方式有些不同。他没有先站到讲台后面，而是径直走向前排，把手中的平板电脑递给了一位同学。「请你大声读一下屏幕上的这段话。」教室里安静了下来。
text.en: Prof. Russell enters differently today. Instead of going behind the lectern, he walks straight to the front row and hands his tablet to a student. 「Please read aloud what's on the screen」. The classroom falls silent.

text.zh: 那位同学开始朗读：「1973年，斯坦福大学的心理学教授马库斯·韦伯发表了一篇开创性论文《认知弹性与决策模型》，首次提出了双通道决策理论……」读到一半，同学停了下来，抬头看向教授——因为他从来没听说过这篇论文，也没听说过这个教授。
text.en: The student begins reading: 「In 1973, Stanford psychology professor Marcus Weber published a groundbreaking paper, Cognitive Flexibility and Decision Models, which first proposed the dual-channel decision theory..」. Halfway through, the student pauses and looks up at the professor — because he's never heard of this paper, or this professor.

text.zh: 不存在的。马库斯·韦伯这个人不存在。那篇论文不存在。双通道决策理论不存在。这整段话是一个大型语言模型生成的，每一句都语法正确、逻辑连贯、细节丰富，而且完全是编造的。这就是我们今天要讨论的问题：AI的{可信度}。或者更准确地说，AI在不应该被信任时，为什么看起来如此值得信任。
text.en: None of it exists. Marcus Weber doesn't exist. That paper doesn't exist. Dual-channel decision theory doesn't exist. This entire passage was generated by a large language model — every sentence grammatically correct, logically coherent, rich in detail, and completely fabricated. This is what we're discussing today: AI {trustworthiness}. Or more precisely — why AI looks so trustworthy when it shouldn't be.

text.zh: 这种现象在技术上被称为「幻觉」，指的是AI生成看似合理但事实上错误的内容。但我想让你们从对齐的角度来理解它。语言模型的训练目标是什么？是预测下一个最合理的词。请注意，是「合理」，而不是「真实」。模型从来没有被训练去关心真相。它被训练去生成人类觉得「像真的」的文本。从这个角度看，幻觉并非一个意外的缺陷，它其实是训练目标的直接结果。
text.en: This phenomenon is technically called 「hallucination」 — AI generating content that seems plausible but is factually wrong. But I want you to understand it through the lens of alignment. What's the language model's training objective? Predict the most plausible next token. Note — 「plausible」, not 「true」. The model was never trained to care about truth. It was trained to generate text that humans would find 「seems real」. From this perspective, hallucination isn't an accidental flaw — it's a direct consequence of the training objective.

text.zh: 这让我想起第一节课的内容，也就是对齐问题的本质。我们想让AI提供准确的信息，但我们训练它做的是生成合理的文本。「准确」和「合理」大部分时候重合，但在关键时刻却会分裂。一个真实但违反直觉的事实，比如量子力学中的某些结论，模型可能会避开，因为它「看起来不太合理」。而一个编造的但看起来非常合理的故事，比如刚才那段，模型会毫不犹豫地生成。
text.en: This reminds me of our first lesson — the essence of the alignment problem. We want AI to provide accurate information, but we train it to generate plausible text. 「Accurate」 and 「plausible」 overlap most of the time but diverge at critical moments. A true but counterintuitive fact — like certain conclusions in quantum mechanics — the model might avoid, because it 「doesn't look very plausible」. While a fabricated but very plausible story — like the one just now — the model generates without hesitation.

text.zh: 面对幻觉问题，你觉得最有效的技术方向是什么？
text.en: Facing the hallucination problem, what do you think is the most effective technical direction?

text.zh: 让模型在回答前先检索外部知识库——用真实资料来约束生成
text.en: Have the model retrieve from external knowledge bases before answering — constrain generation with real sources

text.zh: 这就是{检索增强生成}，简称RAG。思路很直接：与其让模型凭记忆回答，不如让它先去查资料。模型收到问题后，先在知识库中搜索相关文档，然后基于检索到的内容来生成回答。这大幅降低了幻觉率，因为回答有了可追溯的来源。目前这是工业界最广泛采用的方案。但它也有局限：搜索不到正确文档怎么办？检索到的信息本身有错怎么办？模型在综合多个来源时仍可能产生幻觉。
text.en: This is {retrieval-augmented generation}, or RAG. The idea is straightforward: instead of having the model answer from memory, have it look things up first. After receiving a question, the model searches a knowledge base for relevant documents, then generates an answer based on what it found. This dramatically reduces hallucination rates because answers have traceable sources. It's currently the most widely adopted solution in industry. But it has limits: what if the right document can't be found? What if the retrieved information itself is wrong? The model can still hallucinate when synthesizing multiple sources.

text.zh: 让模型验证自己的推理——生成答案后自己检查逻辑链条
text.en: Have the model verify its own reasoning — check its logic chain after generating an answer

text.zh: 这个方向很有前途。链式思维验证的核心思路是：先让模型展示它的推理过程，然后让它（或者另一个模型）检查推理的每一步是否成立。这比直接判断最终答案的正确性要可靠得多——因为推理步骤可以独立验证。就像数学证明一样，你不需要直觉知道结论是否正确，你只需要检查每一步推导是否有效。这是把验证问题分解成更小的、可检查的子问题。
text.en: This direction is very promising. The core idea of chain-of-thought verification: first have the model show its reasoning process, then have it (or another model) check whether each step of reasoning holds. This is much more reliable than directly judging the final answer's correctness — because reasoning steps can be independently verified. Like a mathematical proof, you don't need intuition about whether the conclusion is correct; you only need to check whether each derivation step is valid. This decomposes the verification problem into smaller, checkable sub-problems.

text.zh: 教模型认识自己的知识边界——对不确定的事情诚实地说「我不知道」
text.en: Teach the model to recognize its own knowledge boundaries — honestly say 「I don't know」 when uncertain

text.zh: 这直接关联到一个关键概念：{校准}。一个校准良好的系统，当它说「我有90%的把握」时，它确实在90%的情况下是对的。当它不确定时，它会告诉你。目前的大型语言模型在这方面做得很差——它们用同样自信的语气说出正确的事实和编造的故事。训练模型学会说「我不知道」或者「我对这个不太确定」，在技术上被称为不确定性量化。这可能是解决信任问题最根本的方向。
text.en: This directly connects to a key concept: {calibration}. A well-calibrated system, when it says 「I'm 90% confident」, is actually right 90% of the time. When it's uncertain, it tells you. Current large language models are terrible at this — they use the same confident tone for correct facts and fabricated stories. Training models to say 「I don't know」 or 「I'm not very sure about this」 is technically called uncertainty quantification. This may be the most fundamental direction for solving the trust problem.

text.zh: 这三个方向，即检索增强、推理验证和不确定性校准，并不互斥。工业界最好的系统通常会同时使用所有三种方法。但让我指出一个更深层的问题。
text.en: These three directions — retrieval augmentation, reasoning verification, uncertainty calibration — are not mutually exclusive. The best systems in industry typically use all three. But let me point out a deeper issue.

text.zh: 我称之为「信任悖论」。用户倾向于信任听起来自信的AI——但恰恰是那些最自信的回答可能最不可靠。如果模型在不确定时表现得不确定，用户可能会觉得这个AI「不够聪明」转而使用另一个更自信但更不准确的产品。市场压力推动AI变得更自信，而更自信意味着更不诚实。这是一个系统性的激励错位。
text.en: I call it the 「trust paradox」. Users tend to trust confident-sounding AI — but the most confident answers may be the least reliable. If the model appears uncertain when it is uncertain, users might think this AI 「isn't smart enough」 and switch to another product that's more confident but less accurate. Market pressure pushes AI toward more confidence, and more confidence means less honesty. This is a systemic incentive misalignment.

text.zh: 信任悖论指出：市场激励让AI变得更自信，但这可能降低准确性。你认为该如何打破这个困境？
text.en: The trust paradox shows that market incentives push AI toward more confidence, which may reduce accuracy. How do you think we should break this cycle?

text.zh: 通过监管要求——强制AI系统标明不确定性级别
text.en: Through regulation — require AI systems to indicate uncertainty levels

text.zh: 监管确实可以改变激励结构。如果法律要求AI在医疗、法律和金融领域必须标注置信度，那市场竞争就不会只比「谁更自信」，而是比「谁更可靠」。欧盟的AI法案已经在朝这个方向走了。但监管的难题在于执行：你怎么验证一个AI系统标注的「85%置信度」是否真实反映了它的不确定性？校准本身就是一个技术难题。而且监管往往滞后于技术发展。
text.en: Regulation can indeed change the incentive structure. If laws require AI to indicate confidence levels in medical, legal, and financial domains, market competition wouldn't just be about 「who sounds more confident」 but 「who is more reliable」. The EU AI Act is already heading in this direction. But regulation's challenge is enforcement: how do you verify that an AI system's stated 「85% confidence」 truly reflects its uncertainty? Calibration itself is a technical challenge. And regulation typically lags behind technological development.

text.zh: 通过用户教育——让人们学会质疑AI的输出
text.en: Through user education — teach people to question AI outputs

text.zh: 用户素养确实至关重要。如果所有人都知道AI会产生幻觉，他们就不会盲目信任。但指望所有人都成为批判性思维的专家是不现实的。而且即使你知道AI可能出错，当一个回答写得足够好、足够详细、足够自信时——你的批判能力会下降。这是认知心理学中的流畅性效应：信息呈现得越流畅，人们越倾向于相信它。教育是必要的，但仅靠教育解决不了系统性问题。
text.en: User literacy is indeed crucial. If everyone knew AI produces hallucinations, they wouldn't blindly trust it. But expecting everyone to become critical thinking experts is unrealistic. Even if you know AI can be wrong, when an answer is written well enough, detailed enough, confident enough — your critical capacity drops. This is the fluency effect in cognitive psychology: the more fluently information is presented, the more people tend to believe it. Education is necessary but can't solve systemic problems alone.

text.zh: 通过设计——让AI在界面上清晰区分已验证和未验证的信息
text.en: Through design — have AI clearly distinguish verified from unverified information in the interface

text.zh: 这是一个非常务实而且可以立即执行的方向。如果AI的每一段回答都标注了信息来源和置信度，比如「这个事实来自维基百科」「这段推理我有较高把握」「这个数字我无法验证」，那么用户就有了判断的依据。好的设计可以在不降低用户体验的情况下传达不确定性。让诚实成为一种用户界面特征，而非一种劣势。这需要技术和设计的协同，但方向是对的。
text.en: This is a very pragmatic direction that can be implemented immediately. If every part of AI's answer is annotated with sources and confidence — 「this fact is from Wikipedia」, 「I have high confidence in this reasoning」, 「I cannot verify this number」 — users have a basis for judgment. Good design can convey uncertainty without degrading user experience. Making honesty a UI feature, not a disadvantage. This requires coordination between technology and design, but the direction is right.

text.zh: 回到对齐的主线。幻觉问题告诉我们一件深刻的事情：仅仅让AI「有帮助」是不够的。一个有帮助但不诚实的AI，可能比一个没帮助的AI更危险——因为你会依赖它，然后被它误导。可信度应该是AI设计的第一优先级，在有用性之前。
text.en: Returning to the alignment thread. The hallucination problem tells us something profound: merely making AI 「helpful」 is not enough. A helpful but dishonest AI may be more dangerous than an unhelpful one — because you'll rely on it, then be misled by it. Trustworthiness should be the first priority in AI design, before helpfulness.

suggestedContent.zh: 幻觉是一个对齐问题：模型被训练生成「合理」的文本，而非「真实」的文本。三个技术方向：第一，检索增强生成，也就是先查资料再回答。第二，链式思维验证，重点检查推理步骤。第三，校准，目标是让AI准确报告自己的不确定性。这里存在一个信任悖论：市场激励往往让AI表现得更加自信，而不是更加诚实。核心原则是，可信度应当排在有用性之前。
suggestedContent.en: Hallucination is an alignment failure: the model is trained to generate 「plausible」 text, not 「true」 text. Three technical directions: (1) Retrieval-augmented generation — look things up before answering (2) Chain-of-thought verification — check reasoning steps (3) Calibration — have AI accurately report its uncertainty. Trust paradox: market incentives push AI toward confidence over honesty. Core principle: trustworthiness should come before helpfulness.

text.zh: （拿回平板电脑，看了一眼屏幕上那段编造的文字）我保留这段文字，每次讲到这个话题就拿出来给新学生看。迄今为止，没有一个学生在第一次听到时意识到它是假的。问题不在学生，而在系统。一个不知道自己不知道什么的系统，配上一副无比自信的声音，这简直是信任的天敌。下节课我们来谈伦理。当AI足够强大时，它带来的问题早已超出了技术层面。
text.en: (Takes back the tablet, glances at the fabricated passage on screen) I keep this passage and show it to new students every time I teach this topic. So far, not a single student has realized it was fake on first hearing. That's not the students' fault — it's the system's fault. A system that doesn't know what it doesn't know, paired with an utterly confident voice — that is the natural enemy of trust. Next lesson we'll talk about ethics. When AI is powerful enough, the problems it creates go beyond the technical.

text.zh: 罗素教授把平板电脑滑进公文包里，在教室门口停了一下。他没有回头看，但你听到他轻声说了一句：「在你信任一个声音之前，先问问它是否值得被信任。」门关上了。教室里的金色光线在白板上投下一道长长的影子。你看着自己的笔记，心想——也许最重要的技能是学会在什么时候不相信它。
text.en: Prof. Russell slides the tablet into his briefcase and pauses at the classroom door. He doesn't look back, but you hear him say softly: 「Before you trust a voice, ask whether it deserves to be trusted」. The door closes. Golden light casts a long shadow across the whiteboard. You look at your notes and think — perhaps the most important skill isn't learning to trust AI, but learning when not to.
